mainEntity.name: How does pricing work for electrical troubleshooting in Tysons, VA?

acceptedAnswer.text: We come to the house, look at the actual work, and give a written estimate before any repair starts. Diagnostic visits include most minor on-the-spot repairs. Major repairs get a separate written estimate. No charge for the diagnostic visit in our primary service area.

mainEntity.name: How quickly can you come out for a troubleshooting call in Tysons?

acceptedAnswer.text: Same-day or next-day in most cases during weekday business hours. Tysons is about 4 miles from our Fairfax Blvd office — roughly 10–15 minutes via Route 123 or I-495. If your situation is urgent — burning smell, sparking, warm walls — we will triage you to the earliest available slot and tell you what to shut off in the meantime.

mainEntity.name: What is included in a troubleshooting visit?

acceptedAnswer.text: A real diagnostic — not a guess. We use a multimeter, circuit tracer, AFCI/GFCI tester, and IR thermal camera if heat is suspected. We open panels, test circuits at rest and under load, trace the fault to its source, then explain what we found in plain English before any repair starts.

mainEntity.name: When should I call an electrician versus trying to fix it myself?

acceptedAnswer.text: Call an electrician if you smell burning, see sparking, feel warm walls or warm switch plates, have a breaker that trips daily, or have lost power to part of the house without a clear cause. Resetting a tripped breaker once is fine. Resetting it three times in a row is a fire risk.

mainEntity.name: What is the most common electrical problem in Tysons homes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Breaker trips on overloaded circuits. Tysons' residential areas span three distinct eras — 1950s–1960s ramblers near Pimmit Hills with original 100-amp panels, 1970s–1980s colonials in Westpark and Tysons Woods with 150-amp panels and occasional aluminum wiring, and 2010s luxury rebuilds near Scotts Run with modern 200-amp panels. The older homes were never wired for today's loads; even the 1980s homes struggle with EV chargers, home offices, and heat pump conversions. The second most common call is warm outlets in 1970s homes — usually aluminum wiring connections that have oxidized over decades.

mainEntity.name: Do you handle EV charger problems?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. EV charging puts continuous high-amp draw on circuits that Tysons' older residential homes were not wired for. If your charger throttles, trips a breaker, or warms the outlet, the cause is almost always upstream — a feeder, a breaker, or a connection that cannot sustain the load. We diagnose the cause and either repair it or quote you for the right circuit.
